soil-found-049.title: Soil organic matter in the global carbon cycle
soil-found-049.text: The largest amount of carbon on land is stored in soil organic matter, not in living plants. It holds about four times as much as plants, and world soils hold two to three times the atmosphere's amount. Seven inches of soil with 1% organic matter holds as much carbon as the air above a field. The carbon held in the world's soils is estimated at 2,500 gigatons, 3.3 times the 750 gigatons in the atmosphere and 4.5 times the 560 gigatons in living things. Organic carbon, mostly as {{ref:soil-found-045}}, accounts for about 1,550 gigatons. The rest is inorganic, mainly carbonates and bicarbonates. Plants remove carbon dioxide from the air using sunlight and build organic molecules. Plants and animals release it again by respiration, and burning fuels adds more. As organic matter is depleted the soil becomes a carbon dioxide source. Clearing and burning forest, then rapid loss under agriculture, gives a secondary, often larger flush. Agricultural conversion of forests and grasslands is second only to fossil fuel burning as a contributor to rising atmospheric CO2. Soils managed to build organic matter can become net carbon sinks. It is no silver bullet, but on a massive scale it can slow CO2 increase for a while and also helps the soil bounce back from storms and dry spells.

soil-found-051.title: Soil texture: the sand, silt and clay recipe
soil-found-051.text: Rub a moist pinch of soil between your fingers and you are already measuring its texture. Soil texture is the quality of a soil set by its make-up of sand, silt and clay particles. It considers only particles less than two millimetres across. Texture classes rest on the percentages of the three; the USDA and WRB systems use 12 classes and the UK-ADAS system 11. {{ref:soil-hist-011}} proposed the first classification, the international system, in 1905. Texture can be judged by feel or measured, for example by the {{ref:soil-phys-050}}, which rests on Stokes' law. Because it is fixed by the mineral part of a soil, it does not change with farming, unlike {{ref:soil-phys-001}}. Texture matters because it shapes so much else. {{ref:soil-water-177}}, the soil water content best suited to plant growth, rises as particles get finer, from sand to clay. Texture helps decide which crops suit a soil and predicts its response to drought or its lime needs. Together with structure it is called a master variable, since it directly influences many other properties. A clayey soil has more surface area, capacity for {{ref:soil-chem-047}}, total porosity and organic matter than a sandy one, but less macroporosity. The first of these traits comes from {{ref:soil-found-040}}, and the proportions of all the components are laid out in {{ref:soil-found-078}}.

soil-found-062.title: Mineral hydration, water's first grip on a crystal
soil-found-062.text: Before water can take a crystal apart, it has to attach to it. In mineral hydration, water molecules, or H+ and OH− ions, attach rigidly to the atoms of a mineral. The minerals of {{ref:soil-chem-163}} turning into iron hydroxides, and anhydrite hydrating to gypsum, are examples. Bulk hydration matters less than dissolution, {{ref:soil-form-172}} and oxidation. But hydration of the crystal surface is the crucial first step in it. Water at a fresh surface splits into H+ and OH−. Protons then replace the positive ions at the surface, freeing them. Loosened bonds release silicic acid and aluminum hydroxides. In the mineral of {{ref:soil-form-141}}, this starts at defects on the crystal surface, in a layer only a few atoms thick.

soil-found-063.title: Lichens, roots and microbes that wear down rock
soil-found-063.text: Two common minerals, albite and {{ref:soil-chem-226}}, weather twice as fast in live soil as in sterile soil. Living things make the difference. Biological weathering is weathering started or sped up by soil microorganisms, lichens and plant roots. Soil organisms make up about 10 mg/cm3 of typical soils. Lichens are among the most effective agents. In a New Jersey study, hornblende granite under lichen weathered three to four times faster than bare rock. Most commonly, plants release carbon dioxide along with chelating compounds, chemicals that grip metal ions, such as organic acids and {{ref:soil-bio-192}}. Roots can raise carbon dioxide to 30% of all soil gases. The chelating acids strip metal ions, especially aluminum and silicon, from rock. Where they build up, they can reshape whole soils. Partnerships help too. Root-dwelling fungi free nutrients from minerals such as {{ref:soil-form-144}} or apatite and pass them to trees, and some bacteria weather minerals in ways that promote plant growth. Life also works by force. Seedlings and roots growing in crevices push rock apart, and lichens pluck mineral grains loose with their hyphae, their thread-like filaments.

soil-found-081.title: From food to foundations: how people use soil
soil-found-081.text: Soil resources produce 98.8% of the food humans consume. In farming, soil anchors plants and is their primary nutrient base. The kind of soil and the moisture available decide which plants can be grown. Yet soil is not strictly essential. Systems that grow plants in water or mist, with no soil at all, show as much. Soil is also the foundation for most construction and the basis of many building materials. Surface mining, road building and dam construction move massive volumes of it. Waste treatment relies on soil too. Septic systems, covered in {{ref:soil-env-195}}, and wastewater spread on land both use soil processes that need oxygen, and landfills use soil as daily cover. Water percolating down to become groundwater is filtered on the way, losing pesticides, hydrocarbons, heavy metals and excess nutrients. Organic soils are a significant fuel and horticultural resource, and drained peatlands are farmed in Nordic countries. Animals and humans even eat soil-like substances, a habit called geophagy. Some monkeys eat soil with their leaves to ease tannin toxicity.

soil-found-086.title: What the sky drops into the soil
soil-found-086.text: After water itself, nitrogen is the most abundant ingredient of rain. The reason is that water vapor uses tiny airborne particles, called aerosols, to form droplets. Rain is one of three main inputs the pedosphere receives from the air. The others are wind-blown sediment and gases diffusing in. Wind carries aerosols, pollen and dust into soils, a process called eolian sedimentation. Gases move both ways. Carbon dioxide from roots and microbes keeps the bicarbonate in soil water far above balance with the air. Together with dissolved metals, this makes the soil more acid. Gases escape back to the air from dissolving carbonates, decay, chemical reactions and microbial {{ref:soil-hist-147}}.

soil-found-096.title: The ground rules pedologists use to explain soils
soil-found-096.text: Much of the world's shale began as soil. Soils are natural clay factories, and their clay, eroded into ocean basins, later hardened into rock. Pedologists explain how soils form with a set of working principles. The first is that external factors drive the processes that form soil and create soil patterns. Five major factors dominate: climate, organisms, relief, the rock or sediment beneath, and time. Complexity is more common than simplicity, and today's soils carry imprints of past processes that may be hard to observe. Those processes create and destroy order within a soil, often at once, and its layers record the balance. Uniformitarianism, the idea that present processes also ran in the past, applies too: they have worked since organisms first appeared on land. Few soils are geologically old. Most date no further back than the Pleistocene. Knowing soil genesis aids classification, mapping and management. Yet classifications cannot rest on genesis alone, since its processes are seldom observed and change over time.

soil-found-119.title: Mineralogy, the science of how minerals are built
soil-found-119.text: Talc sits at one end of a scale and diamond at the other. Mineralogy is the branch of geology that studies the chemistry, crystal structure and physical properties of {{ref:soil-found-029}}, optical ones included. It asks how minerals form, how to classify them, where they occur and how people use them. Some crystallize from molten rock deep in the crust; others grow as rock weathers at the surface or in soil. Identification starts with a hand sample. Hardness is a first clue, ranked on the Mohs scale from talc at 1 to diamond at 10. {{ref:soil-chem-228}}, shown in 1912, later revealed crystal structures.

soil-meth-013.title: Near-infrared spectroscopy, a quick scan for soil tests
soil-meth-013.text: Near-infrared light travels deep into a sample before it is absorbed. Near-infrared spectroscopy uses the part of the spectrum from 780 nm to 2500 nm, where absorption comes from weak overtone and combination vibrations. Because the light penetrates far, bulk material can be probed with little preparation. The bands are broad and overlap, so readings need {{ref:soil-meth-034}}, such as principal components or partial least squares, built on carefully chosen calibration samples. Karl Norris at the USDA pioneered it for agricultural products in the 1980s. It is valued as accurate, rapid, non-destructive and inexpensive, and soil-testing laboratories may use near-infrared scanning in a {{ref:soil-fert-187}}.

soil-meth-045.title: Spatial analysis: studying things by where they are
soil-meth-045.text: Spatial analysis is any of the formal techniques that study entities using their topological, geometric or geographic properties. It spans many methods, especially spatial statistics, and covers {{ref:soil-meth-006}}, spatial regression and statistics of {{ref:soil-meth-046}} such as Moran's I and Geary's C. Geographic information systems capture, store, manipulate and analyse spatial data, with map overlay a basic vector operation. Two errors recur. The ecological fallacy draws conclusions about individuals from aggregate data. The locational fallacy is a poor spatial characterisation of the elements. Spatial sampling picks limited locations to measure phenomena that show dependency and heterogeneity; basic schemes are random, clustered and systematic.

soil-meth-052.title: Choosing where to sample for a digital soil map
soil-meth-052.text: A digital soil map is only as good as the sites that train it. The aim of sampling design here is to select sites representative of the geographic area and of the soil-forming factors, the covariates, being modelled. Two families of design exist, building on {{ref:soil-meth-044}}. Geometric designs work on the map. They include grid, simple random, stratified random, transect, cluster and nested sampling. Grid sampling places points at the centre of evenly spaced cells, and stratified random applies random sampling within strata, as in {{ref:soil-meth-048}}. Cluster sampling groups sites closely to cope with rough terrain, and nested sampling quantifies variability at different distances. Feature-space designs work on the covariate values instead. Fuzzy k-means sampling minimises distance in covariate space. A conditioned form of {{ref:soil-meth-040}} (Minasny and McBratney, 2006) samples all covariates with one sample per stratum. An optimal design covers both geographic and feature space.

soil-phys-006.title: Flocculation: how clay particles join and drift apart
soil-phys-006.text: Muddy water that clears in a few hours has usually flocculated. In colloid chemistry, flocculation is when colloidal particles leave suspension as floc or flake. Unlike precipitation, the particles were first merely suspended in a stable dispersion. The IUPAC definition is contact and adhesion that makes larger clusters. This agglomeration is reversible, so the particles can be dispersed again. In dispersed clay slurries, flocs form once agitation stops, because negative face charges attract positive edge charges. Clay plates flocculate when their slightly positive edges stick to the negative faces of other plates. Sodium displacing polyvalent cations weakens this and deflocculates the clay. The forces involved include van der Waals forces, electrostatic forces and hydrogen bonding. Flocculation is the opposite of dispersion, in which particles are held apart. The balance between them is set mainly by soil pH, electrical conductivity and sodium content. It also matters for freshwater: highly dispersible colloids make water turbid and adsorb nutrients that drive {{ref:soil-env-020}}. Floccules become lasting aggregates only once cementing agents stabilize them. The particles involved are the finest of the {{ref:soil-phys-047}}, chiefly {{ref:soil-found-040}} and {{ref:soil-chem-079}}.

soil-phys-032.title: Biological soil crust: a living skin on bare ground
soil-phys-032.text: Across about 12% of the earth's landmass, the ground between plants is covered by a living skin. A biological crust on the soil surface is a community of fungi, lichens, cyanobacteria, bryophytes and algae in the open spaces between vascular plants. Only cyanobacteria and cyanolichens fix nitrogen, so what a crust contributes depends on its makeup. Its carbon cycling happens only when it is wet. Crusts darken the surface, which lowers {{ref:soil-phys-177}}, and their roughness traps dust. The easiest way to keep them is to remove stressors such as grazing, or to protect them from disturbance.

soil-phys-035.title: Timing a water drop: measuring how much soil repels water
soil-phys-035.text: The simplest measure of a stubborn soil is how long one drop of water takes to soak in. Soil water repellency tests rate how strongly a soil repels water, usually starting with that drop. Under 5 seconds means not repellent, up to 1 minute slightly repellent, 1–10 minutes repellent, and longer severely repellent. The molarity of ethanol droplet test tries ethanol solutions of falling {{ref:soil-phys-260}} until one soaks in within 10 seconds. An index of 1 or less means non-repellent, and 2.2 or more severely repellent.

soil-phys-070.title: Five sizes of soil pore, from cracks to cryptopores
soil-phys-070.text: A pore's size decides what water it holds and what can live in it. A widely used grouping, after Brewer (1964), sorts soil pores by diameter. The largest class, {{ref:soil-water-189}}, are over 75 μm, too large for significant capillary force. Unless closed off, they drain and are usually full of air at the wetness described in {{ref:soil-water-177}}. They form where soil cracks, where peds and aggregates separate, and along roots and burrows. Mesopores, 30–75 μm, are the largest pores still full of water at that point. Called storage pores, they hold water that plants and soil organisms can use, so soil scientists study them closely for agriculture and irrigation. Micropores, 5–30 μm, hold water that is practically immobile yet still available to plants, so dissolved substances move through them mainly by {{ref:soil-phys-240}}. Ultramicropores, 0.1–5 μm, shelter microbes inside aggregates from predators such as amoebae and {{ref:soil-bio-193}}, and their volume tracks bacterial biomass. Texture and organic matter set them, and compaction barely touches them. Cryptopores, under 0.1 μm, are too small for most microbes. Organic matter inside them is protected from decay, and their water is barely available to plants.

soil-phys-088.title: Wheels, hooves and tillage: what compacts farmland
soil-phys-088.text: Farmland can compact on its own, through drying and wetting, or under external pressure. Heavy machinery compacts the subsoil as well as the topsoil, and that deeper compaction is harder to reverse. Axle load, speed, number of passes and tyre pressure all set how severe it is. Working the soil can itself compact it, though over the long term it may leave less topsoil compaction than leaving the soil unworked. Heavy trampling by livestock, set by how intensively they graze, is another major cause.

soil-phys-098.title: Pore water pressure, the push of water between grains
soil-phys-098.text: Water held between soil grains pushes back. Pore water pressure is the pressure of the groundwater in the pores between the particles of a soil or rock. Deep in saturated ground it is measured with piezometers. Where the water is not flowing it is close to hydrostatic, rising steadily with depth. The surface where it equals atmospheric pressure is the {{ref:soil-water-247}}. Above that level, capillarity sets the pressure, and it is called tension, suction or matric pressure. Instruments with a porous ceramic cup in contact with the soil measure it there, by methods set out in ISO 11276:1995. The pressure has several parts: the weight of overlying material, {{ref:soil-chem-216}} from uneven ion concentrations, and pressure from water films, held by {{ref:soil-chem-145}}, that draw grains together. It matters because the load carried by the grains, {{ref:soil-phys-100}}, is the total stress minus the pore water pressure. Too much of it can force blocks out at the base of river banks, and rising pressure on slopes helps burst the surface layer, as in {{ref:soil-phys-160}}.

soil-phys-107.title: Cohesion: the strength that is not friction
soil-phys-107.text: Friction explains most of a soil's strength, but not all of it. Cohesion is the part of a soil's or rock's shear strength that does not depend on friction between particles. In soils it comes from electrostatic forces in stiff clays that once bore heavier loads, from cementing by Fe2O3, CaCO3 or NaCl, and from negative {{ref:soil-phys-254}}. The pore pressure response when water cannot drain adds some, and so do plant roots. Several sources are temporary. Weathering can remove electrostatic bonds, wetting removes capillary suction, time dissipates pore pressure, and logging or fire removes root strength. The theory in {{ref:soil-phys-169}} usually measures cohesion as the shear strength at zero normal pressure on the failure surface. Values run from 0 to 48 kPa for very soft clay, through 192 to 384 kPa for stiff clay, to 384 to 766 kPa for very stiff clay. When soil loses cohesion it can slough off banks and slopes.

soil-phys-110.title: Consolidation: the slow squeeze that sinks buildings
soil-phys-110.text: Picture a spring inside a water-filled container with a hole in its lid. Press the lid and at first the water resists. Then it drains out through the hole, and the spring shortens and takes over the load. The spring is the soil skeleton. The process is soil consolidation. It is the gradual change in a soil's volume under a change in pressure, as water is slowly squeezed out of or drawn into its pores. When saturated soil is loaded, the water, far stiffer in volume than the skeleton, first carries the load as excess pore water pressure. As it seeps away, the grains take the load and the soil shrinks. Saturated clays consolidate very slowly, because water passes through them with extreme difficulty. Coarse soils drain readily and settle at once instead. Clays settle under external loads, under their own weight or that of overlying soil, and when groundwater pumping raises the effective stress on them. The effects show most where a building sits on soft, poorly permeable soil such as {{ref:soil-water-298}}, which can settle a great deal over many years. In the narrow sense the term means this delayed, drainage-driven response. In the broad sense it covers any pressure-driven volume change, including compaction, sinking land, heave and swelling. Karl von Terzaghi, the 'father of soil mechanics', defined it as any loss of water from a saturated soil without air taking its place. Engineers measure it with the test in {{ref:soil-phys-170}}, loading a thin disc of soil in steps and recording its thickness over time.

soil-phys-114.title: Terzaghi, Fillunger and a bitter quarrel over consolidation
soil-phys-114.text: The first modern theories of soil consolidation appeared in the 1920s, along two very different lines. Karl Terzaghi's simplified model, built on the {{ref:soil-phys-241}}, became engineering practice. Paul Fillunger's rigorous mixture-theory model was too abstract to apply to real cases. Their bitter dispute ended tragically in 1937 with Fillunger's suicide, and his results were forgotten for decades. Maurice Biot later developed the full three-dimensional theory. Terzaghi's one-dimensional model is still the most used, because it is simple and rests on cheap, reliable oedometer tests.

soil-phys-116.title: Liquefaction: when shaking turns solid ground to liquid
soil-phys-116.text: In the 2018 Palu earthquake, the ground itself flowed. It buried the suburb of Balaroa and Petobo village 3 metres deep in mud. Soil liquefaction is the sudden loss of strength and stiffness in a wet soil of loose, unbound grains. Under stress such as earthquake shaking, the solid behaves like a liquid. Loose sand tends to compress under load. If it is saturated, pore water pressure rises until it exceeds the contact forces between grains, and effective stress falls to essentially zero. Dense sands dilate instead. So the soils most at risk are loose, saturated, poorly drained sands and non-plastic silts; gravels and clays rarely liquefy. Young Holocene beds of well-sorted sand and silt, saturated and metres thick, along stream beds, beaches, dunes and loess areas, are the most susceptible. Allen Hazen first called soil 'liquefied' after the 1918 failure of the Calaveras Dam in California. Engineers paid closer attention after the 1964 Alaska and Niigata earthquakes. Shaking can force water and liquefied sand to the surface, and ground can slide sideways on slopes of only 1 or 2 degrees, called lateral spreading. Liquefaction damages buildings, bridges, buried services and levees. Over geological time it may also leave a dense parent material in which a fragipan can develop. Engineers fight it by densifying soil with vibration or {{ref:soil-phys-237}} or stabilising it with grout, and cementing sand with calcite made by microbes has been proposed.

soil-phys-159.title: Needle ice: frost columns that heave seedlings from the ground
soil-phys-159.text: On a cold night, columns of ice can grow straight up out of bare soil. Needle ice is needle-shaped columns of ice that grow from groundwater at the soil surface. It forms when the soil is above 0 °C but the air at the surface is below 0 °C: water rises by capillary action and freezes onto the growing column. Needles are typically a few centimeters long. Ten centimeters is the recorded maximum, though specimens of 15-20 cm have been seen at Gerðuberg. It needs {{ref:soil-phys-179}}, in which supercooled water freezes onto existing ice in a porous medium, and it favors soils high in silt and organic matter. It is {{ref:soil-phys-153}} at the start of the freezing season, before there is any soil overburden to lift. Taber found that pore size controls the amount of frost heave, and that a gradient of soil moisture tension drives water up toward the freezing front near the surface. Growing needles lift soil particles and crusts, which settle unevenly on melting. They disturb streambanks, aid soil creep and shape patterned ground. They also heave seedlings out of the ground, and the seedlings often die because they do not resettle or their roots dry out. Swedish pipkrake, coined in 1907 by Henrik Hesselman, is one of several names. Others are frost pillars, Kammeis and shimobashira. See {{ref:soil-phys-137}} for the soil temperatures involved.

soil-phys-213.title: Transpiration: how plants lift soil water into the air
soil-phys-213.text: An acre of corn gives off about 3,000–4,000 U.S. gallons (11,000–15,000 liters) of water a day. That flow is transpiration: water moving through a plant and evaporating from its leaves, stems and flowers. It is passive and costs the plant no energy. It also cools the plant and drives the mass flow of {{ref:soil-fert-289}}. Very little of the water roots take up goes into growth; 97–99.5% is lost by transpiration and guttation. Two stretches set the pace. From soil to root, flow depends on the soil's hydraulic conductivity and the pressure gradient through the soil. Up the plant, water moves mainly down differences in water potential. When roots take up less than leaves lose, stomata close. That slows nutrient uptake and limits photosynthesis and growth. The soil's temperature and moisture influence how far stomata open, and roots struggle in dry, very fertile or salty soils. Isotope measurements show transpiration is the larger part of evapotranspiration. They also show transpired water differs from {{ref:soil-phys-203}} and streams, so soil water is less well mixed than assumed. It is measured with potometers, {{ref:soil-water-248}}, porometers, photosynthesis systems and sap flow sensors.

soil-phys-229.title: Three kinds of compaction and how to tell them apart
soil-phys-229.text: Each kind of compaction has different signs and different remedies, so diagnosis comes first. Surface seals show broken-down aggregates, poor seedling emergence and fast runoff and erosion. Sandy loams and silt loams are especially prone, because their unstable aggregates leave small particles that fill pores into dense crusts. Surface layer compaction shows as deep wheel tracks, standing water, cloddy tillage and stubby, crooked roots with few root hairs. A penetrometer, wire flag or shovel dig can confirm it. Freshly plowed soil can falsely look uncompacted because it is loose at first, while no-tilled soil is firmer but has strong structure and worm-made large pores. Subsoil compaction is found with a penetrometer in field-moist soil, which often meets much higher resistance at the base of the plow layer (typically 6 to 8 inches), and by roots that are absent below the pan or run sideways above it. Compacted soil that stays wet becomes anaerobic, causing stunted growth and {{ref:soil-fert-108}} losses shown by yellow leaves. Weakened crops are more prone to root diseases such as Pythium and Fusarium. For background, see {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-230.title: Crops that compact soil and how to offset them
soil-phys-230.text: Some crops are hard on soil. Root and tuber crops, silage corn, soybeans and many vegetable crops compact it through {{ref:soil-agri-097}}, low residue return or wet-soil harvest traffic. Countermeasures include soil-improving rotation crops, extensive cover crops, controlled traffic and extra manure or compost. In an 11-year Vermont trial on clay soil under continuous corn silage, yearly dairy manure of 0, 10, 20 and 30 tons per acre gave pore space of 44%, 45%, 47% and 50% of soil volume.

soil-phys-234.title: Deep tillage: breaking up a plow pan
soil-phys-234.text: Deeper tillage shatters a plow pan or other deep compacted layer so roots can explore deeper. It must be done when the full depth is dry and friable, otherwise it smears the soil. Going below the 6 to 8 inch depth of normal tillage is costly and energy consuming, and does little for surface compaction from aggregate breakdown; narrow-shank zone building or deep strip tillage disturbs less. It works better on coarse soils, because in fine soils the whole subsoil is strong, and tilling wet subsoil can cause smearing and drainage problems. Heavy loads must stay off afterwards to prevent re-compaction, and soils prone to washed-down fines may need repeated deep tillage.

soil-phys-236.title: Managing field traffic to spare the soil
soil-phys-236.text: Most compaction is avoidable if the right passes are changed. Judge traffic by soil moisture at the time and by equipment weight and load distribution. Late dry planting does little damage, but wet-harvest trucks and spring plowing of wet clay loam do much. Tracks greatly reduce subsoil compaction. Multiple axles, and wide tires at low inflation pressure, spread loads, and most compaction comes from the first tire passing. Dual wheels enlarge the footprint but cut subsoil compaction less, because pressure cones merge at shallow depth, and they tempt fieldwork on wet soil. Poorly drained fields suffer worse compaction; {{ref:soil-phys-227}} dries the subsoil, and surface shaping and mole drains suit heavy clay. The problem itself is in {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-237.title: Dynamic compaction: dropping tonnes to densify ground
soil-phys-237.text: Weights of 8 to 36 tonnes are dropped from 1 to 30 metres, and the stress waves can reach up to 10 metres deep. Dynamic compaction is a ground improvement method that densifies soil by repeatedly dropping a heavy weight at regularly spaced points. In cohesionless soils the waves cause liquefaction followed by compaction; in cohesive soils they raise {{ref:soil-phys-098}} before compaction. Results depend on weight, drop height and spacing. Old fills and granular soils are most often treated, and soil below the {{ref:soil-water-247}} needs care to let excess pore pressure escape. It is an engineered form of {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-238.title: Critical state: when soil flows like a frictional fluid
soil-phys-238.text: The branch of soil mechanics called critical state theory models saturated remoulded soils on the critical state concept. At the critical state, stress and strain relate constantly: the soil keeps deforming without any further rise in stress, like a frictional fluid. In practice this marks failure. The concept was published in 1958 by Roscoe, Schofield and Wroth, from Cambridge simple shear tests and Imperial College triaxial tests. The Cam-Clay models assume an isotropic, elasto-plastic soil with no creep, and the Modified Cam-Clay of John Burland uses an elliptical yield surface. It extends the ideas of {{ref:soil-phys-101}} and {{ref:soil-phys-073}}.

soil-phys-248.title: Growing regions: where climate and soil favor a crop
soil-phys-248.text: Some regions are known by a single crop. A growing region is a geographic area whose climate, soil and farming practices favor producing particular crops, plants or livestock. A region may be dominated by one crop, such as the American Corn Belt, or be diverse where the soil is very fertile and seasonal rainfall is high, as in Queensland and New South Wales. Cultivation may be enabled by a regional climate or a unique microclimate, and regions are often aligned along a latitude because crops need consistent climate.

soil-phys-249.title: Soil as solid, liquid and gas
soil-phys-249.text: Soil is never just dirt; it is three things at once. It combines solid, liquid and gas phases, and their interaction determines how it behaves. The solid phase is mineral particles (rocks, gravel, sand, silt, clay) or organic matter, and ideally takes up about 50% of the volume. The liquid phase is soil water plus dissolved nutrients, chemicals and gases, together forming the soil solution; both its quantity and its chemical composition matter. The gaseous phase is soil air, commonly nitrogen, oxygen, water vapour and carbon dioxide. Ideally it is about 25% of volume, but it is highly dynamic. Mass-volume relationships among the three phases define porosity, {{ref:soil-phys-060}} and the shares of water and air in pore space.

soil-phys-250.title: The breakthrough curve: watching a solute emerge from a column
soil-phys-250.text: Feed a solute into one end of a column of porous material and measure what comes out of the other. The result is the breakthrough curve: the course of the solute's concentration at the outlet after a step change in inlet concentration. A fixed bed is purged with a carrier, then the adsorptive is added so that inlet concentration changes in a step, and the outlet concentration is monitored. Chromatography instead uses pulses. Integrating the area above the whole curve gives the material's maximum loading, and the time until the outlet reaches a threshold concentration gives its usable capacity to take up the solute. The curve's shape carries information on mass-transfer properties, which can be found by fitting simplified models to the data. It shows adsorption of the kind described in {{ref:soil-phys-196}} at work. The source page frames this in adsorption engineering; it does not describe the soil-column version.

soil-phys-257.title: Hygroscopy: materials that draw water from the air
soil-phys-257.text: Some materials pull water out of the air and keep it. Hygroscopy is the attracting and holding of water molecules from the surroundings by absorption or {{ref:soil-chem-145}}. Many fertilizer chemicals and salts are hygroscopic, and the moisture they hold is usually proportional to relative humidity. Deliquescent materials absorb enough water to dissolve into a solution, at a characteristic deliquescence relative humidity that depends on temperature and crystalline hydrate form. Soil voids stay saturated with water vapor up to the point of maximal hygroscopicity, beyond which a vapor-pressure deficit develops in the pore space.

soil-phys-258.title: Osmosis: why salty soil starves roots of water
soil-phys-258.text: Salty soil can leave a plant short of water even when the ground is wet. Osmosis explains why. It is the net movement of solvent through a selectively permeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration, which is the same as from high to low {{ref:soil-water-172}}. The pressure needed from outside to stop that net flow is the osmotic pressure. It is a colligative property, so it depends on the solute's molar concentration and not on its identity. Osmotic transport is a pressure-driven viscous flow of solvent, not the random spreading of molecules. In a plant cell, osmotic entry of water raises turgor pressure until it equals the osmotic pressure. In a hypertonic solution water leaves and the cell shrinks; in a hypotonic one it swells turgid. Roots take in water and nutrients across cell membranes by osmosis, so excess salt in the soil lowers water uptake and can cause leaf burn.

soil-phys-259.title: The water molecule and what makes it unusual
soil-phys-259.text: Almost everything water does in soil starts with the shape of one molecule. Water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom in a bent, polar molecule. It can make up to four hydrogen bonds, which explains its unusual thermodynamic properties. Cohesion and adhesion give high surface tension, 71.99 mN/m at 25 degrees C, and capillary action that lifts water over 100 m in trees. Specific heat, the energy needed to warm it, is very high at 4184 J/(kg K) at 20 degrees C, with a heat of vaporization of 40.65 kJ/mol. Density peaks at 3.98 degrees C, so between 0 and 3.98 degrees C water shows an unusual negative thermal expansion. Its high dielectric constant makes water an excellent solvent for hydrophilic substances, but not hydrophobic ones. Over long periods it weathers and erodes rock into soil and sediment.

soil-phys-262.title: Capillary water: held in small pores, only partly usable
soil-phys-262.text: Capillary water is the water held in small soil pores by adhesion and cohesion, the forces behind {{ref:soil-phys-095}}. Only part of it is available to plants. Plant available water is held between field capacity ({{ref:soil-water-177}}) and the point where plants wilt for good ({{ref:soil-water-178}}), in mesopores.

soil-water-003.title: How rain and runoff carry soil away
soil-water-003.text: Almost 36 billion tons of soil are lost to water every year, according to a global model. Water erosion is the removal of soil by rainfall and by the surface runoff it produces, a form of {{ref:soil-water-001}}. It begins with the rain itself. Raindrops bombard aggregates and detach small particles that are easily transported, by splash or by water running downhill, to a low area where they are deposited. Runoff, the flow described in {{ref:soil-water-019}}, begins when the soil is saturated or when rain falls faster than water can infiltrate (see {{ref:soil-water-180}}). Runoff with enough flow energy carries loosened soil particles down the slope as sediment. Rain and runoff cause four main types of erosion, in rising severity: splash, sheet, {{ref:soil-water-025}} and {{ref:soil-water-027}}. Concentrated runoff cuts small channels called rills. If runoff keeps deepening them, they may grow into gullies, a gully being a rill too deep for tillage equipment to smooth. Sheet erosion and rilling cause most soil erosion. The damage is not evenly spread, either. Water erosion removes soil mainly from the middle and lower parts of a slope rather than from hilltops.

soil-water-154.title: How wet soil steadies the weather
soil-water-154.text: Soil moisture shapes more than a harvest. Water has roughly double the {{ref:soil-phys-242}} of soil, so wetter soil warms and cools more slowly under the same heating. Through the soil's temperature, moisture then affects biological triggers such as seed germination, flowering and the activity of soil fauna. The effect reaches the sky. Climate modelling by Timbal and colleagues in 2002 linked soil moisture to the persistence and variability of surface temperature and rainfall in Australia. Soil water now matters for climate modelling and weather prediction, and the Global Climate Observing System lists it among its 50 Essential Climate Variables.

soil-water-155.title: Soil moisture, the quarter of a loam that keeps plants alive
soil-water-155.text: Half of a loam's volume is solid. Gas fills a quarter and water the other quarter, and only about half of that water is available to most plants. The water held in a soil, measured by volume or by weight, is soil moisture. It shapes soil formation, structure, stability and erosion, but its main importance is for plant growth. Water makes up 80–95% of a plant's protoplasm. It carries nutrients as a solvent and keeps plants upright through turgor, the pressure of water inside their cells. Water leaves a field in four ways: as runoff across the surface, as water draining through the soil, by evaporation from the surface and by transpiration from plants. Inside the soil it moves under gravity, {{ref:soil-phys-258}} and capillarity. Entering water drives air out of the largest pores and can burst air-filled aggregates, a process called slaking. Roots empty the largest pores first. Water in the smallest pores clings so tightly to particles that roots cannot take it, so availability depends strongly on texture. Moving water also dissolves solutes and {{ref:soil-chem-154}} and redeposits them lower in the profile, a process called leaching. Probes such as {{ref:soil-water-225}} and {{ref:soil-water-170}} measure soil moisture in place, and remote sensing estimates it from afar.

soil-water-156.title: Saturated and unsaturated flow: pushed by gravity, pulled by suction
soil-water-156.text: Water in soil moves in two quite different ways, and the line between them sits at field capacity ({{ref:soil-water-177}}). Between 0 and 33 kPa suction, up to field capacity, gravity and differences in water pressure push water away from where it was applied. That is saturated flow. At higher suctions the push gives way to a pull. Water's adhesion to soil solids sets up a suction gradient, which draws water from wetter to drier soil and from macropores to micropores. That is unsaturated flow. The lab manual states the same split in other units: saturated flow at tensions of 0 to -0.3 bar, driven by hydrostatic head, and unsaturated flow at 0.3 to 31 bars, driven by a tension gradient. ({{ref:soil-water-172}} explains these suctions.) Unsaturated flow is slow, at most about 2.5 cm a day, so roots keep dying back and growing toward moister soil. It slows because the connected wet pathways shrink as soil dries. {{ref:soil-water-193}} therefore depends on water content, and it falls in a very non-linear way as soil dries. Six factors control infiltration and movement: texture, structure, organic matter, depth to impervious layers such as hardpans or bedrock, water already present, and {{ref:soil-phys-137}}. Warm soils take in water faster, while frozen soils such as permafrost may not absorb it at all, depending on how they froze. {{ref:soil-water-238}} gives the rate of change of moisture in unsaturated soil. Lewis Richardson first published it in 1922, and software such as Hydrus solves it numerically.

soil-water-159.title: Percolation: the slow trickle below the roots
soil-water-159.text: After soil drinks in the rain, gravity keeps pulling. Percolation is the downward drainage of water through a soil after the soil has absorbed it. Water draining through macropores under gravity during rain is called {{ref:soil-phys-261}}. Drainage stops at field capacity, when adhesion and cohesion hold the rest. Once a soil is fully wetted, extra water percolates below the roots. It carries clay, nutrients and contaminants that may pollute groundwater, along with the dark organic material of {{ref:soil-bio-089}}. Magnesium, sulfur and potassium leach most readily, and phosphorus very little. Deep percolation that reaches groundwater is groundwater recharge, and groundwater in turn feeds soil moisture through percolation.

soil-water-175.title: The water retention curve, a soil's moisture signature
soil-water-175.text: In 1907 Edgar Buckingham filled soil columns 48 inches tall with six soils, from sand to clay, and drew the first water retention curve. The curve links a soil's water content to its {{ref:soil-water-172}}. Also called the soil moisture characteristic, it differs between soil types and predicts water storage, plant water supply and aggregate stability. Near zero potential the soil is almost saturated and holds water mainly by capillarity. As it dries, the remaining water is bound ever more strongly, in the smallest pores, at grain contacts and as adsorbed films. Sandy soils release most of their water at higher potentials. Clayey soils, which also bind water through {{ref:soil-phys-253}} and osmosis, release it only at lower ones. At any given potential, peaty soils usually hold far more water than clayey soils, and clayey soils more than sandy ones. Even one soil has two curves. Pores fill and drain differently, so hysteresis, a lag between wetting and drying, gives separate wetting and drying curves.

soil-water-180.title: How rain soaks into the ground, and when it stops
soil-water-180.text: Sand and well-aggregated soils can take in 2.5 cm of rain an hour, while high-clay soils accept as little as 0.25 cm. That intake is infiltration, the process by which water on the ground surface enters the soil. Gravity drives it, helped by capillary forces, absorption and {{ref:soil-phys-258}}. Infiltration capacity is the maximum rate, usually given in meters per day. It lasts only while there is room at the surface, which depends on porosity and on how fast earlier water moves down through the {{ref:soil-phys-069}}. As a storm goes on, that room shrinks. Infiltrated water fills storage and weakens capillary pull. Wetted clays swell and narrow their pores. Raindrops striking bare ground wash fine particles into surface pores. Robert E. Horton suggested that capacity drops quickly early in a storm, then settles to a near-constant value after a couple of hours. When rain arrives faster than the soil can take it in, the surplus usually runs off, unless a physical barrier holds it in place. Rates are measured in the field with devices such as {{ref:soil-water-187}}, permeameters and {{ref:soil-water-256}}.

soil-water-209.title: Hydropedology, where soil science meets hydrology
soil-water-209.text: Hydrology likes to pair with the Earth's other spheres, as hydroclimatology, {{ref:soil-water-240}} and the field in {{ref:soil-phys-208}} show. Hydropedology is the emerging field that joins soil science and hydrology. It studies the interface between the pedosphere and the hydrosphere, the planet's water. Soil hydrology and hydropedology are both listed among the areas of practice of soil science. The biomantle shows what the field studies. Loosened by {{ref:soil-bio-047}}, it speeds downward drainage through biopores and carries throughflow downslope above dense subsoil horizons.

soil-water-235.title: Keeping a checkbook for the water in soil
soil-water-235.text: Some irrigators run their soil like a bank account. The soil water balance method, also called the checkbook method, schedules irrigation by tracking deposits and withdrawals. Rain and irrigation are the deposits. Evapotranspiration, the soil's evaporation plus the plants' transpiration, is the withdrawal. Each day's depletion equals the previous depletion plus crop evapotranspiration, minus rain and irrigation. Crop evapotranspiration is {{ref:soil-phys-217}}, the loss from a standard grass surface, adjusted by a {{ref:soil-phys-218}} set out in FAO Paper 56. Coefficients above 1 mark high water users such as corn, and below 1 drought-tolerant plants such as cactus. The method relies on accurate weather data.
